posts.author: Geezertron
posts.content_md:
I don't know what holo setup you're refering to, buy I had 3M send me some samples of that material (assuming it's the same stuff) about 10 years ago. The plastic sheets were reasonably rigid (similar to cheap polarizing sheets), and I was able to make holos with it..my reasoning being that I'd increase the brightness by reducing the horizontal paralax in a reflection holo.

It worked, but not spectacularly so, and when the viewing angle approached the cut-off point of the louvres, the image got pretty dirty (for lack of a better word) and I didn't bother with it any further.

If you write (or phone) them and tell them you have an idea for integrating their product into holographic applications, they'll likely be happy to send you a few small samples. You won't be the first to ask them, but they'll probably still play ball.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
Brings back memories. 

The material I used to make the hologram viewer was called "light control film" or LCF, made by 3M, and primarily sold for computer privacy, as this is. I don't know if this is the same stuff. 

The viewer (in a modified form) is marketed as the VoxBox by Holorad ([http://www.holorad.com](http://www.holorad.com)), formerly Voxel. The original patent has long since expired, so if this is the same stuff, I'd love to put another box together. It's great for full aperture transmission image plane holograms, and gives a nice monochromatic image.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Kaveh, let's see if I remember correctly. One would shoot an image plane transmission H2 and replay it with white light. The louvers would be placed in front of the film. The viewing angle would be designed to correspond with the louver angle and the 0 order beam would be blocked. This would make a single color by angle selection and would be showing the 1st order image. Is that roughly correct?

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
It works on the principle of two equal and opposite dispersions. 

You need to make a diffraction grating with the same reference angle as the holgoram, say 45°. You put the grating and the hologram together, separated by the light control film. Then you shine the white light straight onto the grating, at 0°. The diffracted (first order) light goes through the louvers, but the undiffracted (0 order) is blocked. The diffracted light goes on to reconstruct the image of the hologram. What you see is a monochromatic, sharp image, as each color of light has undergone an equal and opposite diffraction. The whole assembly is in line with the direction of the white light. 

I have forgotten how to upload an image, but will draw a diagram soon...

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: If I remember correctly, Vikuity (formerly 3M) no longer makes the light control film with a 45 degree angle. The "privacy" film used for computer displays has microlouvers at normal incidence, which prevent viewing from the sides. I believe they also make it with a 30 degree angle too, but not 45. I think Voxel has the only remaining stock at 45 degrees.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md: Sounds right. The 45° one has a much smaller market, and is harder to make too.
